import_contract.diagram_rendering: Resolve diagram_asset_ids against assets. Render the SVG with its viewBox aspect ratio and alt_text.

import_contract.provenance: Textbook references belong to each learning outcome. These parallel practice questions are newly authored, with changed values and contexts.

learning_outcomes.title: Polynomial operations
learning_outcomes.statement: Write polynomials in standard form. Add and subtract polynomials.
learning_outcomes.rule_summary: Order terms by decreasing powers. Combine like terms. When subtracting a polynomial, change the sign of every term in the second polynomial.

learning_outcomes.title: FOIL and binomial products
learning_outcomes.statement: Multiply binomials by using the FOIL method.
learning_outcomes.rule_summary: (a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd. Combine the two middle products when they are like terms.

learning_outcomes.title: Factoring by GCF and grouping
learning_outcomes.statement: Factor polynomials by using the Distributive Property and grouping.
learning_outcomes.rule_summary: Factor out the greatest common factor first. For grouping, arrange terms so both groups contain the same binomial factor.

learning_outcomes.title: Factoring monic trinomials
learning_outcomes.statement: Factor trinomials of the form x² + bx + c.
learning_outcomes.rule_summary: Find integers m and n with m + n = b and mn = c. Then x² + bx + c = (x + m)(x + n).

learning_outcomes.title: Interior angles of polygons
learning_outcomes.statement: Find and use the sum of the measures of the interior angles of a polygon.
learning_outcomes.rule_summary: For a simple n-sided polygon, the interior angle sum is (n − 2)180°. For a regular polygon, each interior angle is (n − 2)180°/n.

learning_outcomes.title: Properties of parallelograms
learning_outcomes.statement: Recognize and apply the properties of the sides and angles of parallelograms.
learning_outcomes.rule_summary: Opposite sides and opposite angles are congruent. Consecutive angles are supplementary. A diagonal divides a parallelogram into two congruent triangles.

learning_outcomes.title: Tests for parallelograms
learning_outcomes.statement: Recognize the conditions that ensure a quadrilateral is a parallelogram.
learning_outcomes.rule_summary: Sufficient tests include both pairs of opposite sides congruent, both pairs of opposite angles congruent, diagonals bisecting each other, or one pair of opposite sides both parallel and congruent.

learning_outcomes.title: Kites
learning_outcomes.statement: Recognize and apply the properties of kites.
learning_outcomes.rule_summary: In a kite with AB = AD and CB = CD, AC is the symmetry diagonal. AC is perpendicular to BD and bisects BD. The opposite angles at B and D are congruent.

learning_outcomes.title: Dilation coordinates
learning_outcomes.statement: Find the scale factor of a dilation.
learning_outcomes.rule_summary: For a dilation centered at the origin, (x, y) maps to (kx, ky). Use image/original to find k, retaining the signs of coordinates.

learning_outcomes.title: Similar polygons
learning_outcomes.statement: Solve problems using the properties of similar polygons.
learning_outcomes.rule_summary: Corresponding angles of similar polygons are congruent. Corresponding side lengths have one common ratio. Match vertices in the stated order.

learning_outcomes.title: Dilation scale factors
learning_outcomes.statement: Find the scale factor of a dilation.
learning_outcomes.rule_summary: Scale factor = image length/original length. For positive k, 0 < k < 1 gives a reduction and k > 1 gives an enlargement. A dilation preserves angle measures.

learning_outcomes.title: AA triangle similarity
learning_outcomes.statement: Identify similar triangles using the AA Similarity Postulate.
learning_outcomes.rule_summary: Two pairs of congruent corresponding angles establish triangle similarity. Parallel lines and vertical angles can supply those angle pairs.

learning_outcomes.title: Proportional parts in triangles
learning_outcomes.statement: Use proportional parts within triangles.
learning_outcomes.rule_summary: A line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides proportionally. A triangle midsegment is parallel to the third side and half its length.

learning_outcomes.title: Parts of similar triangles
learning_outcomes.statement: Recognize and use proportional relationships of corresponding angle bisectors, altitudes, and medians of similar triangles.
learning_outcomes.rule_summary: Corresponding altitudes, medians, and angle-bisector lengths of similar triangles have the same ratio as corresponding sides. Within one triangle, an angle bisector divides the opposite side in the ratio of the adjacent sides.

learning_outcomes.title: Geometric mean
learning_outcomes.statement: Find the geometric mean between two numbers.
learning_outcomes.rule_summary: The geometric mean of positive a and b is √(ab). For a right triangle with altitude h to a hypotenuse split into p and q, h² = pq. A leg squared equals the whole hypotenuse times its adjacent hypotenuse segment.

learning_outcomes.title: Pythagorean theorem and converse
learning_outcomes.statement: Use the Pythagorean Theorem and its converse.
learning_outcomes.rule_summary: For a right triangle, a² + b² = c² with c the hypotenuse. For valid side lengths and longest side c, compare c² with a² + b² to classify the triangle.

learning_outcomes.title: Special right triangles
learning_outcomes.statement: Use the properties of 45°–45°–90° and 30°–60°–90° triangles.
learning_outcomes.rule_summary: 45°–45°–90° side ratio is 1:1:√2. In a 30°–60°–90° triangle, sides opposite 30°, 60°, and 90° have ratio 1:√3:2.

learning_outcomes.title: Right-triangle trigonometry
learning_outcomes.statement: Use trigonometric ratios to find side lengths and angle measures of right triangles.
learning_outcomes.rule_summary: sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan θ = opposite/adjacent. Use inverse ratios for angles. Set a scientific calculator to degrees.

learning_outcomes.title: Angles of elevation and depression
learning_outcomes.statement: Use trigonometric ratios to find side lengths and angle measures of right triangles.
learning_outcomes.rule_summary: Angles of elevation and depression are measured from horizontal lines. Use vertical height differences, including eye height when given.

learning_outcomes.title: Area with two sides and an angle
learning_outcomes.statement: Find the area of a triangle using two sides and an included angle.
learning_outcomes.rule_summary: Area = ½ab sin C, where C is the included angle between sides a and b. If two other angles are given, find the included angle using the 180° sum.

learning_outcomes.title: Special-product factorization
learning_outcomes.statement: Factor binomials that are differences of squares and factor perfect square trinomials.
learning_outcomes.rule_summary: A² − B² = (A − B)(A + B). A² ± 2AB + B² = (A ± B)². Extract the GCF before applying a special-product pattern.

learning_outcomes.title: Interior and exterior angle reasoning
learning_outcomes.statement: a) Prove and use the Polygon Interior Angles Sum Theorem. b) Find and use the sum of exterior angles of a polygon.
learning_outcomes.rule_summary: For a convex polygon, diagonals from one vertex form n − 2 triangles. Interior sum = (n − 2)180°. One exterior angle at each vertex, taken consistently around the polygon, sums to 360°.

learning_outcomes.title: Solving with similar triangles
learning_outcomes.statement: Use similar triangles to solve problems.
learning_outcomes.rule_summary: Establish similarity by AA, SAS, or SSS. Write corresponding vertices in order, set up a proportion, and solve. Check that all lengths use the same units.

learning_outcomes.title: Distance and midpoint in space
learning_outcomes.statement: Use Distance and Midpoint Formulas in Space.
learning_outcomes.rule_summary: Distance = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)² + (z₂ − z₁)²]. Midpoint = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2, (z₁ + z₂)/2).

learning_outcomes.title: Law of Sines and the ambiguous case
learning_outcomes.statement: Determine whether three given measures define 0, 1, or 2 triangles using the Law of Sines.
learning_outcomes.rule_summary: Use a/sin A = b/sin B. For SSA, sin B = b sin A/a. Test both B₁ = sin⁻¹(value) and B₂ = 180° − B₁, accepting only cases with A + B < 180°. Opposite sides and angles share letters.

questions.stem: Write 7 − 4x² + 3x³ − x in standard form.

Simplify (6y² + 2y − 9) − (4y² − 5y + 1).

answer.explanation: Distribute the negative, then combine like terms.

answer.explanation: Subtract the known polynomial from the target.

answer.explanation: The GCF is 4r². The other positive forms are not completely factored.

What is the sum of the interior angles of a nonagon?

What is each interior angle of a regular decagon?

A quadrilateral has angles x°, (x + 20)°, 2x°, and (2x − 20)°. Find x.
A regular polygon has interior angle 165°. How many sides does it have?

answer.explanation: Opposite angles are equal. x=14, so ∠A=64°.

questions.stem: Consecutive angles of a parallelogram are (3x + 10)° and (5x − 6)°. Find x.
Which statement is always true for parallelogram ABCD?

options.text: All four angles are right angles.

questions.stem: A parallelogram has adjacent sides 2x + 1 and x + 4. Its perimeter is 46. Find x.
Which condition guarantees that a quadrilateral is a parallelogram?

options.text: One pair of opposite angles is congruent.
Both pairs of opposite sides are congruent.
One pair of opposite sides is congruent.

answer.correct_option_text: Both pairs of opposite sides are congruent.
answer.explanation: Both opposite-side pairs are required for this test.

questions.stem: AB ∥ CD in quadrilateral ABCD. Which extra fact guarantees a parallelogram?

answer.explanation: The same opposite-side pair must be parallel and congruent.

questions.stem: Diagonals AC and BD meet at E. AE = EC = 7, BE = 3x − 1, ED = x + 9. Which x proves a parallelogram?

answer.explanation: Both diagonals bisect each other when 3x−1=x+9.

questions.stem: Which condition alone is insufficient to prove that a quadrilateral is a parallelogram?

options.text: Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel.
Both pairs of opposite angles are congruent.

answer.explanation: A kite can have perpendicular diagonals without being a parallelogram.

questions.stem: Which angle list, in cyclic order, guarantees a parallelogram?

answer.explanation: Both pairs of opposite angles are congruent.

questions.stem: A student says that congruent diagonals guarantee a parallelogram. Which shape is a counterexample?

answer.explanation: An isosceles trapezoid can have congruent diagonals.

questions.stem: In kite ABCD, AB = AD, CB = CD, ∠A = 80°, and ∠C = 120°. Find ∠B.

answer.explanation: The remaining 160° is shared equally by B and D.

questions.stem: The diagonals of a kite intersect. What is the angle between them?
In kite ABCD, AB = AD and CB = CD. Diagonals meet at E. If BE = 6, find BD.

answer.explanation: The symmetry diagonal AC bisects BD.

questions.stem: In the kite shown, AE = 8, CE = 3, and BE = ED = 6. Find BC.

For a kite with two distinct pairs of adjacent congruent sides, which statement need not be true?

options.text: One pair of opposite angles is congruent.

answer.explanation: Only the symmetry diagonal necessarily bisects the other diagonal.

answer.explanation: Both coordinates are multiplied by the same factor.

answer.explanation: Forward k=3. The inverse uses its reciprocal.

questions.stem: A dilation about the origin sends B(4, −6) to B′(−2, 3). Find k.

questions.stem: One triangle has angles 42° and 68°. Another has angles 70° and 42°. What can you conclude?

options.text: Their side lengths must be equal.
The triangles are similar by AA.

answer.correct_option_text: The triangles are similar by AA.
answer.explanation: The first third angle is 70°, so the angle sets match.

questions.stem: In triangles ABC and DEF, ∠A = ∠D = 50° and ∠B = ∠F = 60°. Which statement matches corresponding vertices?

answer.explanation: Corresponding angles from parallel lines prove AA.

options.text: No. A second matching angle is needed.

answer.correct_option_text: No. A second matching angle is needed.
answer.explanation: One matching angle alone is insufficient.

questions.stem: A 1.8 m person casts a 1.2 m shadow. A nearby pole casts an 8 m shadow at the same time on level ground. Find the pole height.

answer.explanation: h/8=1.8/1.2. The sun creates equal elevation angles.

questions.stem: In a bow-tie figure, AB ∥ DE, and A, C, E and B, C, D are collinear. Why are ACB and ECD similar?

options.text: Vertical angles at C and an angle pair from parallel lines.

answer.correct_option_text: Vertical angles at C and an angle pair from parallel lines.
answer.explanation: These supply two congruent angle pairs.

answer.explanation: The third side is twice the midsegment.

questions.stem: A midsegment has length 3x − 2 and the parallel side has length 8x − 12. Find x.
D lies on AB and E on AC. AD = 4, DB = 6, AE = 6, and EC = 9. Which conclusion follows?

answer.explanation: 4/6=6/9, so use the converse proportionality theorem.

questions.stem: D is on AB and E on AC, with DE ∥ BC. AD = 5, AB = 12, AC = 18. Find AE.
A segment joins the midpoints of two triangle sides. Which statement must be true?

options.text: It is perpendicular to the third side.
It is parallel to the third side.

answer.correct_option_text: It is parallel to the third side.
answer.explanation: This is the Triangle Midsegment Theorem.

questions.title: A • Difference of squares
questions.stem: Factor over the integers and justify every stage.

parts.prompt: Factor 12x² − 75y² completely. Show the GCF and the difference-of-squares step.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: 12x²−75y² = 3(4x²−25y²) = 3(2x−5y)(2x+5y). Award 1 for GCF, 1 for squares, 2 for factors.

parts.prompt: Factor 18a⁴ − 50a² completely.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: 18a⁴−50a² = 2a²(9a²−25) = 2a²(3a−5)(3a+5). Award 2 for GCF and 2 for binomial factors.

parts.prompt: Expand one of your factorizations to verify it.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: For example, 3(2x−5y)(2x+5y)=3(4x²−25y²)=12x²−75y². Award 2 for valid expansion.

questions.title: B • Perfect square or near miss?
questions.stem: Use the middle-term test, including the sign.

parts.prompt: Show that 9t² − 30t + 25 is a perfect square trinomial and factor it.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: 9t²=(3t)², 25=5², and −30t=−2(3t)(5). The factorization is (3t−5)². One mark for each check/factor stage.

parts.prompt: Determine whether 4c² + 12cd + 9d² is a perfect square trinomial. Justify and factor.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: Yes. 12cd=2(2c)(3d), so the factorization is (2c+3d)². Award 2 for test and 1 for factors.

parts.prompt: A student claims 4c² + 10cd + 9d² = (2c + 3d)². Explain the error.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: (2c+3d)² has middle term 12cd, not 10cd. Award 1 for expansion fact and 1 for conclusion.

parts.prompt: Find k so that x² − 18x + k is a perfect square.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: k=(18/2)²=81. Award 1 for method and 1 for value.

questions.title: C • Dimensions and repeated factoring
questions.stem: A rectangular panel has area 4x² − 100 square units, with x > 5.

parts.prompt: Factor the area completely.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: 4(x²−25)=4(x−5)(x+5). Award 1 for GCF and 2 for difference-of-squares factors.

parts.prompt: Give possible positive length and width expressions and verify their product.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: Possible dimensions are 2x−10 and 2x+10. Their product is 4x²−100. Both are positive for x>5. Award 3.

parts.prompt: If x = 8, find those dimensions and the area.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: At x=8 the dimensions are 6 and 26, and area=156. Award 2.

parts.prompt: Factor x⁴ − 81 completely over the integers.

questions.title: A • Build the theorem
questions.stem: Consider a convex polygon with n sides.

parts.prompt: Draw a hexagon. Triangulate it using diagonals from one vertex. Label the triangles.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: A correct convex hexagon has 3 noncrossing diagonals from one vertex, forming 4 triangles. Award 2.

parts.prompt: Use your diagram to explain why the interior angle sum of an n-gon is (n − 2)180°.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: An n-gon forms n−2 triangles. Their angles partition the polygon interior, so the total is (n−2)×180°. Award 3 for count, triangle sum, and conclusion.

parts.prompt: A regular polygon has each interior angle 156°. Set up an equation and find n.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: 156n=180(n−2). Thus 24n=360 and n=15. Award 3.

parts.prompt: Find its exterior angle and check the exterior angle sum.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: Exterior angle=180−156=24°. Check 15×24=360°. Award 2.

questions.title: B • Exterior angles and algebra
questions.stem: A convex pentagon has one exterior angle at each vertex, all measured in the same direction. They are x°, (x + 10)°, (2x − 5)°, (x + 20)°, and (x + 5)°.

parts.prompt: Write an equation using the exterior-angle theorem.
Solve for x.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: 6x+30=360, hence x=55. Award 2.

parts.prompt: Find all five exterior angles and the corresponding interior angles.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: Exterior angles are 55°,65°,105°,75°,60°. Corresponding interiors are 125°,115°,75°,105°,120°. Award 2 per correct list.

parts.prompt: Verify the interior-angle sum for the pentagon.

questions.title: C • Work backward and critique
questions.stem: A designer uses regular polygons in a tiled pattern.

parts.prompt: A regular polygon has exterior angle 18°. Find its number of sides.
Find its interior angle and total interior-angle sum.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: Interior angle=162°. Interior sum=(20−2)180=3240°. Award 1+2.

parts.prompt: A student claims a regular polygon can have each interior angle 145°. Test this claim.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: Its exterior angle would be 35°, giving n=360/35=72/7, which is not an integer. Such a regular polygon does not exist. Award 3.

parts.prompt: Explain why one exterior angle at each vertex of a convex polygon sums to 360°.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: Walking once around its boundary makes one complete turn. The consistent exterior turns sum to 360°. Award 2.

questions.title: A • Nested triangles
questions.stem: In triangle ABC, D lies on AB and E lies on AC. DE ∥ BC. AD = 6, DB = 4, AE = 9, and BC = 15.

parts.prompt: Prove that triangle ADE is similar to triangle ABC.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: ∠DAE=∠BAC (common angle), and ∠ADE=∠ABC (corresponding angles with DE∥BC). Thus ADE~ABC by AA. Award 3.

parts.prompt: Write the small-to-large scale factor.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: AB=6+4=10, so the scale factor is AD/AB=6/10=3/5. Award 1.

parts.prompt: Find AC and EC, showing a proportion.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: 9/AC=3/5 gives AC=15. Therefore EC=15−9=6. Award 2 for proportion/AC and 1 for EC.

parts.prompt: Find DE and the ratio of the two triangle areas.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: DE/15=3/5, so DE=9. Area(ADE):area(ABC)=(3/5)²=9:25. Award 2+1.

questions.title: B • Shadows and unit conversion
questions.stem: A vertical 1.5 m measuring pole casts a 0.75 m shadow. At the same moment, a nearby vertical tower casts a shadow 18 m long on the same level ground.

parts.prompt: Sketch and label the two triangles. Explain why they are similar.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: Two right triangles have equal sun-elevation angles, so they are similar by AA. Award 1 for labeled sketch and 2 for justification.

parts.prompt: Write and solve a proportion for the tower height.
A second pole is 180 cm tall. Predict its shadow length in metres at the same moment.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: 180 cm=1.8 m. Shadow=1.8/2=0.9 m. Award 2.

parts.prompt: State two physical assumptions that support this model.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: Examples include level ground, vertical poles/tower, simultaneous measurements, and parallel sunlight. Award 1 for each of two valid assumptions.

questions.title: C • SSS and SAS reasoning
questions.stem: Triangle ABC has AB = 6, AC = 9, BC = 12. Triangle DEF has DE = 10, DF = 15, EF = 20.

parts.prompt: Use SSS to prove the triangles similar and write a correct similarity statement.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: AB/DE=6/10=3/5, AC/DF=9/15=3/5, BC/EF=12/20=3/5. Thus ABC~DEF by SSS. Award 3.

parts.prompt: A median from A has length 7.2. Find the corresponding median from D.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: The larger median is 7.2×5/3=12. Award 2.

parts.prompt: In a separate pair, XY = 8, XZ = 12, PQ = 10, PR = 15, and ∠X = ∠P = 40°. Prove XYZ ~ PQR.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: XY/PQ=8/10=4/5 and XZ/PR=12/15=4/5. The included angles X and P are congruent, so XYZ~PQR by SAS. Award 3.

parts.prompt: Explain why matching only one angle in the separate pair would be insufficient.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: A single angle can occur in many triangles with different other angles and side ratios. Another valid criterion is needed. Award 2.

questions.title: A • Coordinates and exact distance
questions.stem: Points A(−2, 4, −3) and B(4, −4, 9) are endpoints of a segment in space.

parts.prompt: Find the coordinate changes from A to B.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: Changes are 6, −8, and 12. Award 2 for all three.

parts.prompt: Use the distance formula. Give an exact answer and a decimal to the nearest tenth.
Find the midpoint M.
Find AM exactly and explain its relation to AB.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: AM=√61, half of AB, since M is the midpoint. Award 2.

questions.title: B • Recover an endpoint
questions.stem: A drone travels along a straight segment from P(−3, 2, 5) to Q. Its halfway position is M(1, −1, 4). Coordinates are in metres.

parts.prompt: Write three midpoint equations and find Q.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: (−3+x)/2=1, (2+y)/2=−1, (5+z)/2=4. Thus Q=(5,−4,3). Award 1 for midpoint setup and 1 per coordinate.

parts.prompt: Find the total straight-line flight distance PQ exactly.
Find PM and use it to check your result.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: PM=√(4²+(−3)²+(−1)²)=√26 m. Twice this is PQ. Award 2.

parts.prompt: What would be the units of PQ²?

answer.model_answer_and_marking: Square metres (m²). Award 1.

questions.title: C • Radical coordinates and error analysis
questions.stem: R(√3, 2, 2√2) and S(−2√3, 4, 4√2) are points in space.

parts.prompt: Find the midpoint of RS in exact form.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: Midpoint=(−√3/2,3,3√2). Award 3, one per coordinate.

parts.prompt: Find RS in simplest radical form.
A student adds coordinate changes without squaring them to calculate distance. Explain why that method fails.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: Distance uses squared perpendicular displacements before taking a square root. Signed changes can cancel if merely added. Award 2.

parts.prompt: Find the distance from the origin to T(3, 4, 12), showing the two Pythagorean stages.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: Horizontal distance=√(3²+4²)=5. Space distance=√(5²+12²)=13. Award 2.

questions.title: A • All acute-angle boundary cases
questions.stem: In each case A = 30° and b = 10. Side a is opposite A and b is opposite B.

parts.prompt: Calculate h = b sin A and state its geometric meaning.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: h=10sin30°=5. It is the perpendicular height from the end of side b to the ray carrying side c. Award 2.

parts.prompt: Determine the number of triangles for a = 4, 5, 7, 10, and 12. Explain each classification.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: a=4<h gives 0; a=5=h gives 1 right triangle; 5<a=7<10 gives 2; a=10=b gives 1; a=12>b gives 1. Award 1 per correct classification with its comparison.

parts.prompt: For a = 5, find B and C. Explain why the count is one.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: sinB=10sin30°/5=1, so B=90° and C=60°. The supplementary B equals the same 90°, so it creates no second distinct triangle. Award 3.

questions.title: B • Solve both triangles
questions.stem: Given A = 40°, a = 9, and b = 12. Use degree mode. Keep full calculator precision until your final answers.

parts.prompt: Find sin B and the two candidate values of B.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: sinB=12sin40°/9≈0.85705. B₁≈58.986° and B₂≈121.014°. Award 1 for ratio and 2 for candidates.

parts.prompt: Check both candidates with the angle sum. State the number of triangles.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: 40+58.986<180 and 40+121.014<180, so two triangles exist. Award 2.

parts.prompt: For each valid triangle, find C to the nearest degree and c to the nearest tenth.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: C₁≈81.014°→81°, c₁=9sinC₁/sin40°≈13.8. C₂≈18.986°→19°, c₂≈4.6. Award 1 per requested result.

parts.prompt: Explain why using only the inverse-sine output can miss a triangle.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: An acute and its supplementary obtuse angle have the same sine. Award 1.

questions.title: C • Obtuse angles and false candidates
questions.stem: Use the Law of Sines and the angle-sum condition.

parts.prompt: Given A = 120°, a = 8, b = 10, test the data and state the number of triangles.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: sinB=10sin120°/8≈1.0825>1, so no triangle exists. Award 3.

parts.prompt: Given A = 120°, a = 10, b = 8, determine the number of triangles and solve it. Round angles to the nearest degree and sides to the nearest tenth.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: sinB=8sin120°/10≈0.69282. B₁≈43.854° is valid, while B₂≈136.146° gives A+B₂>180°. Thus one triangle. B≈44°, C≈16°, and c=10sin(16.146°)/sin120°≈3.2. Award 1 for ratio, 1 for rejecting second angle, 1 for count, 1 for angles, 1 for c.

parts.prompt: For an obtuse A, explain why a must be greater than b for a triangle to exist.

answer.model_answer_and_marking: The side opposite the obtuse angle must be the longest side, so a>b. Award 2.
